newsitem.title: POLAND: FEATURE - Poland to tackle bond market liquidity.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Poland to tackle bond market liquidity.

text.p: Poland's bond market, unlike the booming stock and T-bill markets, is still at its teething stage, its development throttled by complicated trading and clearing arrangements despite seven years of market reforms.
It now takes a week and at least two intermediaries for a Polish trader to buy and sell bonds on the secondary market.
But things may brighten up this year as the country's top financial institutions work together to make trade more liquid.
The finance ministry, the National Bank of Poland (NBP) and the National Securities Deposit (KDPW) agree the organisation of the secondary bond market is badly in need of a change.
"The main problem lies with the complicated clearing of the deal," said Grzegorz Raupuk, bond dealer at Bank Gdanski SA.
Under the Polish securities law all bond transactions have to go through brokerage houses, which charge a commission of roughly 0.1 percent of the value of the transaction.

Depending on whether the deal is done between a bank and a non-banking client or with another bank the brokerages can either register the transaction through an off-the-floor bourse deal or directly in the KDPW securities deposit.
Both the bourse and the KDPW charge for their services.
MARGINS CUT BY MIDDLE-MEN AND SLOW SYSTEM
"With all the middle-men taking their commissions, often their total is higher than the spread on the bond," said Wojciech Kowalczyk, dealer at Bank Handlowy SA.

Dealers say their margins are additionally cut by delayed cash flows as payments are made through Bank Slaski SA which is not part of a modern electronic clearing system. Bond liquidity is further reduced by slow transaction confirmations from the KDPW, without which the instruments cannot be re-sold.

"This means that if you buy bonds on Monday with a Tuesday value date you can sell them on Wednesday, and if you do, with a tomorrow/next value date, you would get the cash on Friday," said Krzysztof Kozuchowski, bond dealer at ING Bank in Warsaw.
GOVERNMENT, BANKS URGENTLY NEED LIQUID BOND MARKET

Dealers estimate the monthly turnover on the secondary bond market at between 150 million and one billion zlotys ($325.2 million) compared with some 56 billion zlotys of turnover in secondary T-bill and NBP-bill trade.
The Warsaw bourse's monthly turnover is roughly three billion zlotys.
"It could be a huge market, even bigger than the secondary T-bill market," said Jerzy Stopyra, head of the NBP's monetary policy department.
"For the government it would be the primary source for budget deficit financing and for banks a market for liquid asset management," he said.

The Polish secondary bond market is already largely dominated by foreign investors, trading on fixed-interest two- and five-year bonds, drawn by Poland's good fundamentals. A reform of the system would probably increase their involvement.

Piotr Dziewulski, head of the finance ministry's public debt department, sees a more liquid secondary bond market as one of his priorities for 1997 because it would boost bond sales at primary tenders.

"What we are most unhappy about is not the lack of instruments, not small demand at auctions or high yields, but the organisation of the secondary bond market. We are fully aware that it is not liquid," Dziewulski said.
"We have to do everything to lengthen the maturity of instruments used for public debt financing, and that is one of the reasons why we should make the secondary bond market more liquid," he said.

Although none of the institutions would give a concrete date for when the market could benefit from their combined efforts, they agree the overhaul of the way the market is organised should be speedy.
"Changes should take place this year, hopefully in the summer," said Elzbieta Pustola, the KDPW's president.
DEALERS CALL FOR CENTRAL BANK TO TAKE OVER
Dealers say many of the problems could be solved if the central bank took over from the KDPW the running of a bond deposit for interbank deals, just as it does for T-bill trade.
They also say Poland's current four bond markets -- the bourse's retail and block bond markets, the off-the-floor and the interbank market -- should all be merged into the one run by the NBP.
"The NBP should run a deposit for bank's bonds in the same way it does for T-bills and we should have one market instead of four," said Marcin Rzechowski, bond trader at PBI SA bank.
The NBP believes the KDPW should keep the register of retail bond transactions while the central bank would register turnover for wholesalers.
"If we were to have a wholesale bond market the NBP could participate in the organisation of it and run a register of the transactions," said NBP's Stopyra.
But Pustola said that instead of creating two separate deposits, for individuals and for big players, a simpler way would be to open an account for the KDPW in the NBP's bank account department.
"Since all bonds are paperless this would allow banks' interbank bond deals to be cleared in minutes rather than days," Pustola said.
The NBP seems reluctant to adopt this suggestion partly because the KDPW is not a bank.
The decision about which option to choose lies with the bond issuer -- the treasury -- but Dziewulski said it was still too early to make a final choice.
"I don't know which option is better because we have not yet fully analysed them, but I would like the one which can be implemented faster," Dziewulski said.
($ = 3.075 Polish Zlotys)
